sentences.text: Confuciusornis possessed a toothless beak similar to that of modern birds, which was robust, pointed, and near triangular in side view.
The animal was roughly the size of a modern crow, measuring about 50 cm in total length with a wingspan of up to 70 cm.

It possessed advanced traits like a short tail with a pygostyle and a bony sternum, but retained primitive features such as large forelimb claws, a skull with a closed eye-socket, and a small breastbone.
Several hundred complete specimens of Confuciusornis have been found, making it one of the most abundant vertebrates in the Yixian Formation.
In a 0.5-kilogram individual, the primary wing feathers of Confuciusornis reached 20.7 centimetres in length.
Confuciusornis was the first early bird fossil to show preserved pheomelanosomes, though a second team failed to find these traces.
Researchers suggested that the presence of medullary bone in a Confuciusornis specimen indicated it was a female, as this tissue serves as a calcium reservoir for egg production in modern birds.
A studied female Confuciusornis specimen showed evidence of at least three years of growth, indicating an extended development period similar to non-avian dinosaurs.
The genus Confuciusornis was formally described by Hou and colleagues in 1995.
The discovery of Confuciusornis began in November 1993 when paleontologists Hou Lianhai and Hu Yoaming were shown a fossil bird specimen by collector Zhang He.
The species Confuciusornis chuonzhous was named by Hou in 1997 using specimen IVPP V10919, which was originally a paratype of C. sanctus.
The holotype of Confuciusornis dui (IVPP V11553) is a nearly complete adult skeleton featuring long tail feathers and an impression of a horny beak.
In 1999, researchers suggested Confuciusornis was likely herbivorous based on its upward-curving, non-raptorial beak, although no stomach contents were known at the time.
Confuciusornis possessed large fleshy foot pads and curved claws similar to modern tree-dwelling birds, suggesting it may have had a similar lifestyle.
The flight apparatus of Confuciusornis was more developed than that of Archaeopteryx, with some specimens showing a keel on the sternum similar to that of modern birds.
Confuciusornis may have had a different flight stroke and was likely not capable of flight for extended periods due to its inability to rotate its arm behind the body and smaller sternal keel.

In 2016, Luis Chiappe and Meng Qingjin estimated a maximum egg diameter of 23 mm based on the pelvic aperture of a large specimen, while in 2007, Gary Kaiser argued that the small egg size suggests large clutch sizes.
Paleontologist Dieter S. Peters compared Confuciusornis to the white-tailed tropicbird, noting similarities in long tails, narrow wings, and nesting habits near volcanoes.
Female mate choice in Confuciusornis may have been efficient if males participated in chick care, such as protecting the offspring.
Analysis of fibrous lamellae in Confuciusornis indicates that early birds possessed rapid growth phases and high metabolic rates, contrary to previous acceptance.
Hou assigned Confuciusornis to the family Confuciusornithidae in 1995.
The recognized species of Confuciusornis include C. sanctus, C. dui, C. chuonzhous, and C. suniae, with the latter two possibly being synonyms of C. sanctus.
Confuciusornis lived in China between 125 and 120 million years ago during the Early Cretaceous Period.

Unlike most species found in the Yixian Formation, Confuciusornis jianchangensis was discovered in the Jiufotang Formation, yet Confuciusornis fossils were discovered in both the Yixian and Jiufotang Formations and are part of the Jehol Biota.
It is debated whether two paratype specimens belong to Confuciusornis sanctus because their bones do not overlap with the holotype.

A 2011 statistical analysis suggested that differences in C. dui might be individual variations within C. sanctus rather than distinct species, though the validity remains debated due to the potential loss of the holotype.
